newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Britain, China report progress in Hong Kong talks.
newsitem.headline: Britain, China report progress in Hong Kong talks.

text.p: Chinese and British negotiators working on details of Hong Kong's 1997 handover to Beijing reached agreement on several issues on Wednesday, the first of three days of talks, the British team leader said.
The negotiators met against a backdrop of disputes over a subversion law drafted by Britain and Chinese troop deployments ahead of the capitalist territory's handover in 209 days.
Britain's chief negotiator in the Joint Liaison Group (JLG), Hugh Davies, told reporters after the session that the two sides agreed on a number of issues.
"We have indeed managed to reach some agreements today. We are not going to tell you what those agreements are at this stage. They will be announced on the last day in a normal way," Davies said.
China's JLG team leader, Zhao Jihua, described the talks as "sincere, pragmatic and in-depth".
Hong Kong's decision last week to draft a liberal anti-subversion law has infuriated Beijing, which said it would not brook major unilateral changes by the British in the countdown to the transition.

The bill itself, which amends Hong Kong's laws covering subversion, secession, sedition and treason, passed its first hurdle in the Legislative Council on Wednesday to enter the queue of pending legislation to be tackled in the weeks ahead.
By making clear the offences entail violence and not mere oral dissent, the draft bill sets legal markers against China-style jailings of dissidents.
British officials said they believed the bill had a good chance of passing.
Pro-Beijing lawmakers, however, vowed to vote against it and some pro-democracy independents reported mixed feelings.

Hong Kong reverts to China at midnight next June 30 when more than 150 years of British colonial rule end under the terms of a treaty in which China pledged to maintain the territory's freedoms and capitalist way of life.

Hong Kong's Democrats expressed their concerns about the future to visiting U.S. Assistant Secretary of State Winston Lord. They accused Washington of taking a softer line on human rights abuses in China in the interests of trade.

The Democratic Party, Hong Kong's largest, said it had expressed worries about the possible eroding of freedoms in Hong Kong and about China's plans to dissolve the elected Legislative Council and install a provisional legislature.

In the latest of many twists in the transition, Britain's Senior Trade Commissioner, Francis Cornish, said on Tuesday that London could not give consular protection to the more than 135,000 Hong Kong people granted British passports recently.
In a concession to widespread demands for full British citizenship following Beijing's 1989 crackdown, London offered passports to 50,000 heads of households.
Cornish said China regarded these people as holders of dual citizenship and would not recognise British consular protection for them on Chinese soil.

Earlier this week, British experts said they had failed to reach agreement with China in the JLG on Beijing's demand to send an advance party of People's Liberation Army (PLA) troops to Hong Kong before the handover.
The events surrounding the PLA's bloody crackdown around Beijing's Tiananmen Square in 1989 remain branded into collective memories in Hong Kong.
